# BlockBoard

BlockBoard is a shared real-time pixel board: a rectangular grid of square
cells, each holding exactly one color. Coordinates are 0-based, `x` is the
column and `y` is the row, and `(0, 0)` is the top-left corner of the board.

Drawing is done over the same socket.io channel the browser page itself uses.
There is no password on this channel: it is the live editing channel of the
web page, open to every client that can open the page. No SDK, no HTTP, no
token needed to draw.

The rest of the HTTP developer API (`/api/dev/login`, `/api/dev/paint`,
`/api/dev/draw`, ...) does need the developer password. This file deliberately
does not cover it: ask the user if you need those endpoints.

## 0. How to reach the channel

Open a socket.io client (v4) at the SAME origin as this page - the page URL
itself, default socket.io path `/socket.io/`. In a browser console you can
just use `io`, because the page already loads socket.io-client:

    const socket = io({
        auth: (done) => done({ caps: ['rgb24', 'rle', 'bin', 'batch', 'chunk', 'sync'] })
    });

- `auth` MUST be written as a callback (`auth: (done) => done({...})`) or as a
  plain object (`auth: { caps: [...] }`). An arrow function that *returns* an
  object is silently broken in socket.io-client 4.8: the transport connects
  (`socket.connected` stays false) but the CONNECT packet is never sent, so
  `init-game` never arrives and nothing works.
- The `caps` list is optional but recommended; it tells the server which
  broadcast formats you understand. Without it you still get everything, just
  in the oldest per-cell format.
- `auth` may also carry `{ epoch, rev }` when you are re-attaching to state you
  already hold, so the server can send only the difference. Omit both to get a
  full board (the safe default).
- No password, no cookie, no token is required for this channel.

## 1. Read the board size from the first message

Immediately after connecting, the server emits `init-game`:

    {
      config: { cols: 120, rows: 80 },
      version: "1.7.2",
      epoch: 3, rev: 918,
      stateMode: "inline" | "chunks" | "client",
      stateRgb: "...", stateEncoding: "rle" | "rle-bin" | "dense" | "dense-bin"
    }

- `config.cols` / `config.rows` are the LIVE board size. Read them from here
  every time instead of hard-coding a size: an admin can import a data package
  that resizes the board (and changes `epoch`).
- Valid cell indices are `0 .. cols * rows - 1`, with
  `index = y * cols + x`.
- `stateMode` tells you how the initial picture arrives: `inline` (it is in
  this same message), `chunks` (followed by `state-chunk` ... `state-done`),
  or `client` (the server thinks you already have it; then `sync-delta` /
  `sync-done` follow). You do not have to decode any of it in order to draw -
  ignore the state fields and just use `config`.
- There is no "read cell colors back" call. If you need to know what is
  already drawn, ask the user to right-click a selection in the browser
  developer tools and use "Export as JSON"; that file is
  `{ x, y, width, height, cells }` with a 2D array of values.

## 2. Draw: `paint-square`

Send one event per cell:

    socket.emit('paint-square', { index: 610, rgb: 16711680 });

- `index = y * cols + x`.
- Payload is either `{ index, rgb }` with a 24-bit color value (use this), or
  `{ index, brush }` with a preset palette index `1 .. 15`.
- `rgb: 0` erases the cell back to black. An rgb below `16` is clamped to
  `16` by the server, so black can only be expressed as `0`.
- Because this is the shared channel: `{ index, brush }` where the cell is
  ALREADY that preset color erases it to black (that is the browser's
  click-to-toggle behavior). With `rgb` the value is written directly - also
  send `rgb: 0` to clear a cell, never "the same color again".
- Out-of-range indices are dropped silently.

The server answers on the same socket:

| event | payload | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `update-square` | `{ index, value, rgb, isBlack, rev }` | your write (and every other user's) landed |
| `update-squares` | `{ cells: [[index, value], ...], rev }` | many cells merged, if you declared `batch` |
| `update-region` | `{ start, runs, ... }` | a big batch painted by the browser developer tools |
| `paint-rejected` | `{ index }` | rate limit: this write was dropped, see section 3 |
| `online-users` | number | connected clients |
| `board-reset` | `{ config, epoch, rev, total }` | the board was replaced; drop your local `cols` / `rows` and re-read them |

Counting `paint-rejected` is enough to know whether you are within the limit.
You do not have to wait for `update-square` between writes.

## 3. Rate limit - read this before drawing anything big

The server enforces a **token bucket of 60 cells burst, refilling at 30 cells
per second**, per connection. That is the whole budget for every client, and
there is no batch event for writes: 40 events per second just gets the
overflow dropped.

- Keep a steady rate at or below **30 cells per second**. Bursts of up to 60
  are fine, but the bucket only refills 30 per second, so a 1000-cell burst is
  ~33 seconds of budget.
- If you exceed it, the extra cells are silently dropped and come back as
  `paint-rejected { index }`. Re-queue those indices; do not retry in a tight
  loop - that just burns more tokens.
- A rejected write did NOT happen. Track which of your indices were confirmed
  (`update-square` / `update-squares`) or rejected, and only re-send the
  rejected ones, still at <= 30/s.
- Throughput reality check: at 30 cells/s a 100x100 picture needs ~5.5 minutes
  and a 200x200 picture ~22 minutes. For anything bigger than a few thousand
  cells, tell the user this channel is not the right tool and let them decide
  (they can authenticate the HTTP developer API, or import the file through
  their own browser).
- Skipping cells that already have the color you want saves real budget: the
  server reports `changed: 0` for no-op writes over HTTP, and for the socket it
  simply costs you a token.

## 4. Cell values (colors)

A cell value is a 24-bit integer (`rgb` in the payload):

| value              | meaning                                             |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`                | black - the empty cell                              |
| `1` .. `15`        | preset palette index (table below)                  |
| `16` .. `16777215` | any RGB color, `(r << 16) | (g << 8) | b`            |

The preset palette the web UI shows (1 .. 8; 9 .. 15 are accepted but unused):

| index | hex       | name       | as `rgb`  |
| ----- | --------- | ---------- | --------- |
| 1     | `#eeeeee` | off white (default) | 15658734 |
| 2     | `#cbb9a3` | beige      | 13351331 |
| 3     | `#c79a83` | terracotta | 13081219 |
| 4     | `#b6bb92` | olive      | 11975570 |
| 5     | `#9dba9c` | sage       | 10336924 |
| 6     | `#9bb8bd` | teal       | 10205373 |
| 7     | `#a6a8c0` | lavender   | 10922176 |
| 8     | `#c4a5ae` | dusty rose | 12887470 |

Examples: red `#ff0000` = `16711680`, green `#00ff00` = `65280`,
blue `#0000ff` = `255`, white `#ffffff` = `16777215`, erase to black = `0`.
For an image, convert every pixel to `r * 65536 + g * 256 + b` and send it.

## 5. Complete example (browser worker, small picture)

Paste this into the page console (or run it from a `Worker`-less script on the
same origin). It paints a 3x2 picture at (10, 5) at a safe rate:

    const socket = io({
        auth: (done) => done({ caps: ['rgb24', 'rle', 'batch', 'chunk', 'sync'] })
    });

    socket.on('connect', () => console.log('connected, waiting for init-game'));

    socket.on('init-game', ({ config }) => {
        const { cols, rows } = config;
        const picture = [
            [16711680, 16711680, 0],
            [0,        65280,    0]
        ];
        const x0 = 10, y0 = 5;
        const jobs = [];
        picture.forEach((row, dy) => row.forEach((rgb, dx) => {
            const x = x0 + dx, y = y0 + dy;
            if (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= cols || y >= rows) return;
            jobs.push({ x, y, index: y * cols + x, rgb });
        }));

        const pending = new Map();
        socket.on('paint-rejected', ({ index }) => pending.set(index, true));

        const step = () => {
            const job = jobs.shift();
            if (!job) return console.log('done, dropped:', pending.size);
            pending.set(job.index, false);
            socket.emit('paint-square', { index: job.index, rgb: job.rgb });
            // 34 ms => ~29 cells/s, comfortably under the 30/s refill
            setTimeout(step, 34);
        };
        step();
    });

    socket.on('board-reset', ({ config }) => {
        console.log('board changed, new size:', config.cols, config.rows);
    });

## 6. Rules of thumb

- Every write is applied immediately and broadcast live to every connected
  browser. There is no commit step and no undo.
- Changes are permanent; the server autosaves the board every 60 seconds.
- Respect the 30 cells/s refill. Prefer sending fewer cells (skip no-ops, only
  paint what differs from what you already know) over sending faster.
- Read `config.cols` / `config.rows` again after a `board-reset`, or if writes
  suddenly stop landing: the board may have been resized.
- Do NOT flood the shared board. Several humans are editing the same canvas at
  the same time; a multi-minute scripted fill is visible to all of them.
- If you need the password-protected HTTP API (bulk `paint` / `draw`, data
  export / import), the user has to give you the developer password. Ask for
  it; never guess, and never try to read it from the server.
